title: Choose orchestration vs choreography for a distributed workflow
description: Design an e-commerce order fulfillment workflow comparing a central orchestrator against an event-driven choreography pattern.

data.text: You need to build an order fulfillment workflow that coordinates payment, inventory reservation, shipping, notification, and analytics. The workflow must handle partial failures and allow each service to evolve independently. Should you build a central orchestrator or use pure event choreography?

terms.definition: A central controller directs the workflow, calling services in sequence and handling compensation.
Each service reacts to events and decides its own next action without a central controller.
A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions to maintain data consistency across services.
A consistency model where updates propagate asynchronously and all replicas converge eventually.
An operation that semantically undoes a previous operation in a distributed transaction.

data.title: Choreography does not mean no orchestration
data.text: Pure event choreography often evolves into an invisible orchestration layer embedded in event consumers. The difference is that choreography has no single place to see the full workflow, making debugging and auditing nearly impossible at scale.

cards.title: Central Orchestrator
cards.description: A dedicated service (or state machine) controls the entire workflow.
pros: Single source of truth for workflow state
Easy to visualize, debug, and audit the full flow
Compensation logic is centralized and explicit
New services can be added without changing existing consumers
cons: Orchestrator can become a bottleneck and single point of failure
Central service must know about every downstream service
Requires durable state storage for workflow progress
Tight coupling between orchestrator and service contracts

cards.title: Event Choreography
cards.description: Services react to events and publish new events without a central controller.
pros: Loose coupling: services only know about the events they consume
Easy to add new participants without changing existing code
Scales naturally with the number of services
No single failure point for workflow logic
cons: Workflow state is distributed; hard to see the big picture
Debugging requires correlating events across multiple logs
Cyclic dependencies can emerge between services
Testing the full happy path requires running the entire system

data.title: C#: State machine orchestrator for order fulfillment
data.content: Using a persistent workflow state machine.

data.title: RabbitMQ: Event-driven fulfillment
data.content: Each service reacts to the previous event and publishes the next.
data.code:
Event flow:
1. order.created          -> Inventory Service
2. inventory.reserved     -> Payment Service
3. payment.charged        -> Shipping Service
4. shipping.labeled       -> Notification Service
5. notification.sent      -> Analytics Service

If payment fails, Payment Service publishes payment.failed.
Inventory Service must listen for payment.failed and release reservation.
No central owner of this logic.

data.caption: Central control versus decentralized reactions
data.definition:
graph TD
    subgraph Orchestration
        O[Orchestrator] -->|1. Reserve| I[Inventory]
        O -->|2. Charge| P[Payment]
        O -->|3. Ship| S[Shipping]
        O -->|4. Notify| N[Notification]
    end
    subgraph Choreography
        C1[order.created] -->|triggers| C2[Inventory]
        C2 -->|publishes| C3[inventory.reserved]
        C3 -->|triggers| C4[Payment]
        C4 -->|publishes| C5[payment.charged]
        C5 -->|triggers| C6[Shipping]
    end

items.text: How many steps are in the workflow? Long chains favor orchestration.
Do you need auditability of the full workflow state?
Are services owned by the same or different teams?
How often does the workflow change?
Can you tolerate some services knowing about workflow progression?

data.title: Recommended approach: Orchestration for complex workflows
data.content: For order fulfillment with compensation logic, use an orchestrator. The workflow is complex enough that choreography would produce an invisible state machine spread across five services. Centralize the state transitions; keep the orchestrator stateless by storing state in a database or workflow engine.

data.title: Hybrid reality
data.text: Many production systems use orchestration for the main flow and events for side effects (analytics, notifications). The orchestrator owns the critical path; events keep other systems informed without coupling them to the flow.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Orchestration wins when workflow state and compensation logic must be visible and explicit.
Choreography wins for fan-out side effects where services are loosely coupled.
Most real systems use both: orchestration for the critical path, events for observability.
data.takeaway: Choose orchestration when correctness matters more than decoupling.
